blocks.en: Hello, young explorers, and welcome back to Michael's Morning Listening!
Today we meet two awesome surprises: grandparent gamers who play like pros, and lightning hotter than the surface of the Sun.
Ready?
Let's go!
In Japan, there is a senior esports team called the Matagi Snipers.
Every player is over sixty years old.
The oldest is seventy-five, and the average age is sixty-seven.
They play a team shooting game called VALORANT, and they practice together on weekday afternoons.
At first, many players did not even know how to use a computer.
Their coach instructed them step by step, starting with how to turn the machine on.
But they did not give up.
They practiced hard and grew stronger after every lost round.
Then came the big test: a match against a senior team from Malaysia.
The Japanese team played calmly, with clever teamwork.
Their win was valid — no cheating, just skill.
"Do not choke under pressure," their coach told them, and they did not.
One player was absent that day, but the team still won two games to one!
Senior gaming is growing everywhere.
In Taiwan, over three hundred and fifty players over fifty-five joined a senior esports contest.
The oldest player there was eighty-eight!
So remember: games are not only for the young — with patience and practice, grandpas and grandmas can be awesome players too.
Now look up at a summer storm.
A lightning bolt flashes across the sky, and a moment later comes thunder.

Here is the amazing fact: the air around a lightning bolt can reach about thirty thousand degrees — about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun, which is only about five thousand five hundred degrees!
How does it happen?
Inside a storm cloud, tiny ice crystals crash into each other again and again, building up electric charge, like rubbing a balloon on your hair.
When the charge grows too big, it has to escape.
It rushes down to the ground in a flash — and that flash is lightning.
The flash is so hot that it turns the air around it into plasma, a super-hot gas.
For a tiny moment, the flash exposes the whole sky.
Then the super-hot air expands fast, and that expansion is the thunder you hear.
Scientists use delicate instruments to measure lightning.
They say one flash lasts less than a second — but in that second, it is hotter than the Sun's surface!
Of course, the Sun's center is far hotter than any lightning bolt.
But the part of the Sun we see — its surface — is cooler than a lightning flash.
So next time you see lightning, remember: you are watching sky fire, hotter than sunshine itself.
Here's today's idiom: 'hit the road.' When you hit the road, you start a trip — you leave and go!
Here's an example: 'The senior team hit the road early in the morning to play their match in another city.' When did you last hit the road for something exciting?
Let's think about our stories: grandparent gamers, and lightning hotter than the Sun's surface.
First: if your grandparents hit the road to play in a game contest, which game would you teach them first?
Second: lightning is hotter than the Sun's surface but lasts less than a second — why does thunder come after the flash, not at the same time?
Talk about it with your family!
That's all for today, young explorers.
Be brave like the senior gamers — and when it is time for your next adventure, just hit the road!
See you tomorrow!
